A.explanation: This uses $F_1 \cos\theta_1$ and $F_2 \cos\theta_2$, which are the components parallel to the gate through the hinge line and produce no moment about the hinge.

B.explanation: Each perpendicular component $F \sin\theta$ times its distance $d$ gives the moment, and both act to turn the gate the same way so they add.

C.explanation: This uses the parallel $\cos\theta$ components instead of the perpendicular components, and incorrectly subtracts the two moments.

D.explanation: This correctly uses $F \sin\theta$ for the perpendicular component but incorrectly subtracts, even though both $F_1$ and $F_2$ turn the gate in the same sense.

hints: Notice that $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are measured between each force and the gate itself, not to the perpendicular, so you must resolve $F_1$ and $F_2$ into along-gate and across-gate parts.
Recall that only the component perpendicular to the gate contributes to the moment about the hinge, given by distance times $F \sin\theta$ when $\theta$ is to the gate.
Check the diagram for the turning sense of $F_1$ at $d_1$ and $F_2$ at $d_2$ to decide whether their moments about the hinge add or oppose.
walkthrough: Look at the top view: the hinge is at one end, with $F_1$ applied at distance $d_1$ at angle $\theta_1$ to the gate and $F_2$ applied at distance $d_2$ at angle $\theta_2$ to the gate.
State the rule for a moment about a point: moment $=$ magnitude of force perpendicular to the body times perpendicular distance from the point, so $M = d \times F_{\perp}$.
Resolve each force: the component along the gate is $F\cos\theta$ and passes through the hinge line with no turning effect, while the component across the gate is $F\sin\theta$ and causes rotation.
Form each moment: moment due to $F_1$ is $d_1 \times F_1 \sin\theta_1$ and moment due to $F_2$ is $d_2 \times F_2 \sin\theta_2$.

Both pushes act on the same side of the gate and push the gate the same rotational way about the hinge, so the total moment is the sum $(d_1 \times F_1 \sin\theta_1) + (d_2 \times F_2 \sin\theta_2)$. This is option B.
